title: The White Lotus Does Not Whisper
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 23 of 40
content:
The White Lotus did not whisper, but they lowered their voices when I entered. The back room during white lotus visitors carried the smell of tiles, and Ba Sing Se woke around us in cart wheels, shutters, and distant voices. I had learned that Iroh's shop was never merely a shop. It was refuge, theater, kitchen, meeting place, and sometimes a place where an old general pretended he had no past. I had also learned that pretending was different from lying. Today I wanted to know which one he asked of me.

The plan was to decide whether I belonged in the hidden part of Iroh's life. Iroh made difficult things sound easy because he believed they deserved a calm beginning. He poured tea, straightened a chair, and turned a practical task into a small ceremony. I let him do it for a while. Then I asked what part belonged to him and what part belonged to me. His eyebrows lifted. I had learned not to mistake that expression for surprise. Often it meant he was delighted to be challenged.

The complication was already there: old allies treated Iroh like a symbol, and symbols rarely answer whether they are lonely. It arrived without announcing itself, as important things often did. Iroh's posture changed first. The hand holding the cup became still. His smile remained, but it was no longer doing all the work. He moved between jokes and strategy, becoming dangerous only when innocents were threatened. I watched the old power move beneath the surface and waited for him to decide what kind of man he wanted to be in front of me.

I did not wait passively. I refused to leave and asked what he wanted me to know. Iroh had been trained to notice what people needed before they said it. I wanted to be more difficult than that. I wanted to say what I needed aloud and let him answer as a partner rather than a teacher. His gaze softened when I did. Not with pity. With recognition. There was a difference, and I was beginning to trust it.

We returned to the Dragon of the West story he never told straight. Iroh told the story in pieces, allowing ordinary details to matter. He remembered the light, the tea, and the foolish thing someone had said. He did not use wisdom to smooth every rough edge. Some memories were still sharp. I reached for his hand only after asking. He turned it over and threaded his fingers through mine. The gesture was small. The trust inside it was not.

“A secret may protect a person but cannot build intimacy alone.” Iroh said.

The work continued around us. We moved through tiles, coded glances, and calm power as though the objects had been waiting for our conversation to finish. Iroh could make a room deliberate by changing a chair's angle. He could make a meal memorable by adding one spice. He could also forget to sit. I put a cup in front of him and called it an order. He bowed. “At last,” he said, “someone recognizes my need for supervision.”

I told him what I saw when he was not performing wisdom. He introduced me as someone whose judgment he trusted. Iroh had lost a son, a nation he once believed in, a throne he never wanted, and years to a war that taught the wrong definition of strength. He rebuilt himself through tea, laughter, food, music, and the decision to help one frightened nephew become better. I did not want to replace any of that. I wanted to be welcomed into the life after it.

Once the visitors left, I reached for his hand and he squeezed it.

The White Lotus stone sat beside his cup, a small welcome without demands.

I kept the White Lotus stone beside my cup. It felt like a welcome, not an obligation. We kissed once more in the quiet, then closed the door and let the city go on without us. We kissed once more in the quiet, then closed the door and let the city go on without us.
